hook: Clocks fall back today, but time zones were invented by railroads, not government.
beats: Before 1883, every town set its clocks by the sun, so noon changed from town to town.
On November 18, 1883, US and Canadian railroads reset their clocks to four zones, making a Day of Two Noons.
Congress only made standard time zones official law in 1918, thirty-five years later.
question: Would you keep the clock change or end it?
title: Railroads Invented Your Time Zone, Not the Government
source: Library of Congress, 'The Day of Two Noons' (Business History research guide)

hook: Those Leonid shooting stars are mostly grains of sand, not rocks.
beats: The Leonids come from Comet Tempel-Tuttle, which sheds dust along its orbit every 33 years.
Those tiny grains hit our atmosphere at about 44 miles per second, fastest of any major shower.
At that speed, the air in front of each grain superheats and glows, making the bright streak.
question: Have you ever seen a shooting star?
title: Shooting Stars Are Mostly Specks of Sand

trend: Perseverance rover sets Mars driving record
hook: Perseverance just drove a record 28 miles on Mars, where sunsets are blue.
beats: On Earth, air scatters blue light away, so our sunsets look red and orange.
Mars is the opposite: its sky is full of fine dust that behaves differently.
The dust turns the daytime sky butterscotch, but the glow around the setting sun looks blue.
question: Would you watch a Mars sunset?
title: Sunsets on Mars Are Blue, Not Red
source: NASA Science (Mars Exploration Program, rover sunset images)

hook: Voyager 1 is so far away that a message takes a full day.
beats: On November 18, the probe will be 16.1 billion miles away, one full light-day.
Radio signals travel at light speed, so a command takes 24 hours to arrive.
Its reply takes another day. After 49 years, it has covered just 0.0027% of the way to Proxima Centauri.
question: Would you wait 2 days for a text reply?
title: Voyager 1 Is So Far, Messages Take a Whole Day
source: NASA Science (Night Sky Notes) and NASA JPL Voyager mission

hook: Tonight's Taurid fireballs come from a comet that circles the Sun every 3.3 years.
beats: That comet is Encke, and NASA lists its 3.3-year orbit as the shortest of any known comet.
Each trip near the Sun, its ice warms up and sheds dust and gravel along its path.
Every autumn, Earth crosses that trail, and bits hit our air at about 17 miles per second.

stat.label: Comet Encke's trip around the Sun

question: Have you ever seen a real fireball?
title: Tonight's Taurid Fireballs Come From a 3.3-Year Comet
source: NASA Solar System Exploration (2P/Encke) and Britannica (Encke's Comet)

hook: Before this month's supermoon: the Moon is slowly escaping Earth, about 1.5 inches every year.
beats: Mirrors left by Apollo astronauts reflect lasers, so scientists measure the Moon's distance to within millimeters.
A supermoon happens when the full Moon reaches the closest point of its oval orbit.
Ocean tides steal Earth's spin energy and pass it to the Moon, pushing it outward.
question: Will you go out and watch the supermoon?
title: The Moon Is Slowly Drifting Away From Earth
source: NASA (Apollo lunar laser ranging results; NASA Science, What's Up November 2026)

trend: Canadian astronaut spacewalk on the space station
hook: Today's spacewalkers on the space station see 16 sunrises every single day.
beats: The International Space Station zips around Earth at about 17,500 miles per hour.
That speed lets it circle the whole planet roughly every 90 minutes.
Each lap passes through one sunrise and one sunset, so a day lasts only 90 minutes of light and dark.
question: Could you sleep with 16 sunrises a day?
title: Astronauts See 16 Sunrises Every Day

trend: Moon meets Venus in the sky Nov 7
hook: Venus is so bright you can spot it in broad daylight.
beats: Venus is wrapped in thick clouds of sulfuric acid that act like a giant mirror.
Those clouds bounce back roughly 70 percent of the sunlight that hits them.
Earth reflects only about 30 percent, so Venus outshines every star and planet.
question: Have you ever spotted Venus in daylight?
title: Why You Can See Venus in Broad Daylight
source: NASA Science, Venus Facts and Solar System Exploration

trend: NASA exploring a rescue plan for Hubble
hook: As NASA plans to save Hubble, remember it launched blurry from a hair-thin mistake.
beats: Hubble's main mirror was ground too flat by about one fiftieth of a human hair.
That tiny error made light focus in the wrong spots, so its first images came back fuzzy.
In 1993, astronauts fitted Hubble with corrective mirrors, basically eyeglasses for a telescope.
question: What's the smallest mistake that caused you big trouble?
title: Hubble Launched Blurry From a Hair-Thin Mistake
source: NASA Science (Hubble Optics) and Smithsonian National Air and Space Museum

trend: Hera probe visits NASA's DART asteroid
hook: Humans once bumped an asteroid and shortened its orbit by 32 minutes.
beats: NASA's DART spacecraft hit the small moonlet Dimorphos at about 14,000 miles per hour in 2022.
Its orbit around the bigger asteroid shrank from 11 hours 55 minutes to about 11 hours 23.
Rock blasted off the surface acted like a rocket, giving extra push beyond the crash itself.
question: Should we test this on another asteroid?
title: We Changed an Asteroid's Orbit by 32 Minutes

trend: Mars and Jupiter pair up before dawn
hook: Mars and Jupiter look like neighbors, yet sit 370 million miles apart.
beats: Astronomers call it a conjunction. It's only a line-of-sight trick, based on where Earth sits.
This month, Mars is about 121 million miles from us. Jupiter is about 489 million.
Jupiter still outshines Mars because it is far larger, even though it's roughly four times farther.
question: Will you wake up early to see them?
title: Mars and Jupiter Look Close. They're 370 Million Miles Apart
source: NASA Science, What's Up: November 2026 Skywatching Tips (science.nasa.gov)
